title: Latino ocean politics joins cultural inheritance, public access, household cost and cross-partisan climate action
source_unit: 2026 National Azul Poll: Latinos and the Ocean

observations.period: August 7–September 8, 2026; national poll of Latino voters

denominator.unit: Latino voters in the United States

ocean_candidate_vote_lift.unit: percent saying a candidate supporting stronger coastline and ocean policies would make them more likely to vote for that candidate

republican_latino_ocean_candidate_vote_l.unit: percent of Republican Latino voters reporting the same

democratic_latino_ocean_candidate_vote_l.unit: percent of Democratic Latino voters reporting the same

climate_serious_problem.unit: percent agreeing climate change is a serious problem that will affect people’s lives

observations.method: BSP Research poll commissioned by Azul; interviews in English or Spanish, with national Latino-voter sample and regional oversamples; reported overall margin of error +/-2.1 percentage points.
observations.uncertainty: This is a commissioned poll by an ocean-justice advocacy organization; the public release does not provide a full weighting or questionnaire audit here, and vote-likelihood responses are not validated vote behavior.
observations.subgroup: Latino voters overall, with Republican and Democratic subgroup comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Environmental issue salience may be activated by the poll framing or advocacy context; cross-partisan agreement does not imply agreement on implementation, regulation, or party choice overall.

observations.period: August 7–September 8, 2026; climate, ocean and pollution priorities

denominator.unit: Latino voters in the United States

environment_personally_important.unit: percent saying environmental issues such as pollution and global warming are personally important

plastic_pollution_action.unit: percent supporting doing more to prevent plastic pollution

plastic_treaty_support.unit: percent supporting a legally binding international treaty to end plastic pollution

observations.method: BSP Research poll commissioned by Azul; national Latino-voter sample with English/Spanish interviewing.
observations.uncertainty: These are stated concerns and policy preferences, not measures of exposure, behavior, willingness to pay, or implementation feasibility.
observations.counterinterpretation: High environmental salience may coexist with competing economic priorities; stated treaty support does not establish knowledge of treaty design or international enforcement.

observations.period: August 7–September 8, 2026; energy transition and household-cost tradeoff

denominator.unit: Latino voters in the United States

offshore_drilling_ban_renewables.unit: percent supporting banning offshore drilling and replacing it with renewable fuels such as solar and wind

offshore_ban_despite_cost.unit: percent supporting an offshore-drilling ban even if it meant paying more per month for gasoline and household gas

clean_ocean_economy_quality.unit: percent saying clean beaches and oceans are essential to the economy and quality of life

observations.method: BSP Research poll commissioned by Azul; policy preference question includes a stated monthly fuel-cost tradeoff.
observations.uncertainty: The hypothetical cost premium is not quantified; responses cannot estimate actual energy-burden tolerance, distributional incidence, or support after a real price change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may support conservation in principle while opposing specific projects, taxes, siting decisions, or regressive costs; the tradeoff item is a commitment signal, not a revealed preference.

observations.period: August 7–September 8, 2026; cultural inheritance, public access and ocean labor rights

denominator.unit: Latino voters in the United States

ocean_family_traditions.unit: percent saying the ocean is important to maintaining family traditions and culture

beaches_parks_open_everyone.unit: percent agreeing government should maintain beaches and parks open to everyone

all_beaches_public.unit: percent agreeing all beaches should be open to the public

forced_labor_fishing_body.unit: percent supporting an international body to identify forced labor in fishing and sanction noncompliant countries

illegal_fishing_enforcement.unit: percent supporting stronger enforcement against illegal fishing

observations.method: BSP Research poll commissioned by Azul; public-access, cultural, fisheries-enforcement and labor-rights questions reported in the release and issue briefs.
observations.uncertainty: The poll combines domestic access, cultural meaning and international labor-governance preferences; it does not measure actual beach access, seafood purchasing, worker conditions, or knowledge of enforcement institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support for public access and labor protection may be broad civic principle rather than an organized constituency preference; actual implementation can produce local tradeoffs among conservation, recreation, extraction and working waterfronts.

related_sources.claim: Azul publication page containing the poll release, issue briefs, sample, field dates, and policy findings.

boundary: This record adds a Latino cultural-environmental politics route: environmental concern becomes candidate preference, stated willingness to absorb an unspecified energy cost, public-access claims, family tradition, and transnational labor-rights governance. The poll is commissioned by an advocacy organization and measures stated attitudes, not validated voting, observed behavior, actual costs, or realized ocean protection.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Azul publication page was reviewed for the national sample, field dates, language, subgroup, margin-of-error, environmental, energy, public-access, cultural, fisheries and labor-rights findings.
